chapter_title: Concerning the Four Things over which People kill each other
chapter_note: This chapter contains no identifiable cosmological-correspondential substrate. Teaching purity is 0.000 throughout. The four-fold enumeration of destructive human impulses (food obsession, sexual desire, wealth, war/glory) is systematic but describes human behaviors, not cosmic architecture — no domain-to-domain mapping is present. The chapter reads as a unified editorial moral teaching: enumerate worldly vices (paras 2-5) → summarize (para 6) → contrast with Manichaean faith via first-person address including Mani's self-reference as 'this physician' (para 7) → conclude with impermanence warning (para 8). While four-fold enumerations can be substratic, the absence of any cosmic-correspondential content, zero substrate vocabulary, and the moral-applicative purpose of the whole sequence point to editorial composition throughout.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Opens with standard dialogue frame formula 'Once again he speaks to his disciples.' The topic statement 'There are four major things in the world over which all people on earth kill each other' is substantive but introduces a moral teaching, not a cosmological one. No cosmic domains named. Classified as dialogue_frame because the substantive content is moral, not cosmological — the instruction to preserve cosmological questions does not apply here.

First enumerated vice: food obsession. Systematic and impersonal, but describes human behavior (eating, bodily swelling), not cosmic architecture. No correspondential mapping present — no cosmic domain is correlated with another. The enumeration marker 'The first thing is...' could suggest older teaching, but the content lacks any cosmological-correspondential dimension. Classified as editorial_bridge: worldly description serving the chapter's moral purpose. Genuinely uncertain — could preserve traces of an older moral tradition, but nothing diagnostic supports substrate classification.
Second enumerated vice: sexual intercourse/fornication. Heavily lacunose. Same pattern as para 2 — systematic enumeration of worldly behavior without cosmic mapping. No substrate vocabulary.

Third enumerated vice: wealth and pride. 'Useless riches in which they shall pride themselves' — moral judgment language. Descriptive of human behavior, not cosmic structure. No correspondential content.

Fourth enumerated vice: war, disputes, tyranny, pursuit of fame. 'So that they have received a name in the world' — describes worldly glory-seeking. Longest of the four enumeration units. Still entirely in the human-behavioral register with no cosmic mapping. 'Tyranny' and 'received a name in the world' are observations about social power, not cosmic correspondences.

Summary paragraph generalizing about people who pursue the four things. 'On every tongue in the world' — editorial universalizing language. Transitional between the enumeration (paras 2-5) and the soteriological application (para 7). Serves the editorial structure of the chapter.

Clear layer shift: 'However, I say to you' — first-person address to audience. 'This physician whom I have brought' — Mani's self-reference, biographical/institutional. 'He separates the light from the darkness' uses cosmic language but in service of soteriology, not cosmic description. 'Only-begottenness, godliness and obedience' — devotional/institutional virtues. 'Surpasses all people who run after these four worldly things' — moral comparative judgment. Unambiguously late editorial/exhortative layer.

Moral conclusion about impermanence: 'they will not remain with them for eternity; rather they shall leave them behind and die.' Standard devotional closure contrasting worldly transience with spiritual permanence. Completes the exhortative sequence begun in para 7.
